extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century English readers; readers of The Spectator and readers of moral/social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Short moralizing periodical essays and character-sketches that expose social vices and prescribe conduct, using anecdotes, letters, and satire for a general urban readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper devotion with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion itself, however warm, may disorder the mind unless its heats are tempered with Caution and Prudence; keep Reason as cool as possible and guard against the influence of Passion, Imagination, and Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If devotion is not checked by reason it can lead to disorder; the author counsels moderation and vigilance against excessive religious feeling. Example/anti-pattern: indulging 'raptures and extasies' that ignore prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid religious enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion without the check of Reason is apt to degenerate into Enthusiasm; when one imagines a Divine impulse it leads people to slight human ordinances and refuse established forms of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against the thought that one's devotions are 'blown up by something Divine', which produces imaginary raptures and rejection of public worship. Treat claims of direct divine guidance with scepticism and require conformity to reasoned norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superstition is excessive religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition is the Excess not only of Devotion but of Religion in general — contrasted with Enthusiasm (excess of devotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines and contrasts enthusiasm (akin to madness) and superstition (akin to folly); both are weaknesses of human reason that expose people to scorn. Use this distinction when diagnosing religious error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware institutional ritual becoming empty show
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs and ceremonies, once admitted into a church or institution, often stick for ever and degenerate into empty show (illustrated by habits of dress and lengthy ceremonies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that successive officeholders add accoutrements rather than reform; anti-pattern: valuing form over substance, e.g., long ritualized dressing that overwhelms the office's purpose. Use to critique institutions that preserve ridiculous practices by habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piety should be steady and masculine but moderate
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so glorious as a strong, steady masculine Piety, setting aside practical advantages; yet enthusiasm and superstition are its weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value consistent, reasoned piety while rejecting excessive fervour. Emphasize steady moral character rather than theatrical devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use character portraits to warn (set up 'scarecrows')
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering a vicious character not generally known, draw it at length and set it up as a Scarecrow to make an example and warn the ignorant and unwary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial method: detailed satire/character sketch serves as public warning. Practical writing guidance: identify a vice, illustrate it with anecdote and exposition, and generalize to public moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of birth or fortune must be supported by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever advantages of Fortune, Birth, or other Good people possess, they should show collateral Eminences (merit and virtue) besides those distinctions; otherwise distinctions only preserve decency and ceremony, not real esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of those who rely solely on rank: social esteem requires corresponding personal qualities (prudence, equal behaviour, readiness to protect). Use concrete domestic examples to demonstrate failure when merit is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good masters conduct: prudence, equal behaviour, protect and cherish servants
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not only paying wages and giving commands that constitutes a master of a family; Prudence, equal Behaviour, with Readiness to protect and cherish them entitle a man to that character in servants' hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standards for household leadership — avoid ruling by fear alone; cultivate fairness and paternal care. Anti-pattern: expecting obedience from dependants purely by terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority unsupported by merit rests on artifice and flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: All superiority which is not founded on Merit and Virtue is supported only by Artifice and Stratagem: flatterers, make-bates, distant relations and indigent followers sustain humoursome rich men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis of social decay: those without merit gather sycophants who insulate them from reality. Use this to explain why certain social figures maintain undeserved status and to advise readers to value merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid household spies and informers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Spy is entertained in a family, the peace of that house is banished: spies never give account of good services, represent mirth as Wantonness and Disorder, and create jealousy and misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for household management: employing spies undermines trust, reduces masters to cyphers, and breeds contempt. Example: petition from servants describing harms of spies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to illegitimate children — provide education and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have brought children into the world by indirect methods should care for their offspring, give them such an education as may render them more virtuous than their parents, and make some provision for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral prescription: atonement for wrongs is to educate and provide for spurious children; social shame should attach to lewdness, not innocent children. Practical remedy rather than mere condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice requires less effort to cure than to gratify
rubrics_metrics.description: Libidinous men expend extraordinary industry and stratagems to gratify their passions; they might conquer corrupt inclinations with half the pains they use in gratifying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument for self-control: redirect the energy spent on vice into restraint. Use humour and illustration (e.g., 'Cat and a Whoremaster will find a Way through bars') to show the foolishness of such industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning habitual libertinism: public punishment or exile
rubrics_metrics.description: As a proposed punishment for habitual propagators of illegitimate offspring, banish them (after second or third offence) to colonies to people those parts lacking inhabitants; less extreme than death used elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests a public-policy remedy as deterrent and public good — example of using social penalties to reform vice. This is a prescriptive, not merely descriptive, criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic conduct: restraint and clarity of roles
rubrics_metrics.description: On matters of love, the letters advise restraint and moral notice: 'Things are so far advanced, that we must proceed; ... it will be becoming in me to appear still your Lover, but not in you to be still my Mistress. Gaiety in the Matrimonial Life is graceful in one Sex, but exceptionable in the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive norms about propriety in courtship and marriage: lovers should temper expectation and be mindful of gendered social conventions. Use epistolary examples to illustrate proper and improper behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and self-denial preserve esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a call to value and esteem those who set a moderate price upon their own Merit; modesty preserves character as frugality preserves fortune — those who take as much as they can will find opinion of them lessen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: keep desires, words and actions within the regard you observe your friends have for you; avoid claiming more than your merits warrant. Anti-pattern: over-claiming produces social loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions are fallacious; avoid pretence of merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Although people form opinions from first appearances (a man's countenance), that way of raising an opinion is fallacious; do not rely on outward profession alone to establish character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against basing esteem on appearance; encourage demonstrating collateral virtues (courage, activity) to justify claims of gentility rather than mere assertion of birth or rank.
